findings.title: Negative cached checks re-query permissions for every distinct resource
findings.body: When cached permissions do not allow a request, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the user/anonymous permission paths no longer consult permCache before querying the permission store. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent combination. Consequently, checking N distinct resources that a user legitimately cannot access causes N permission-store queries, even though the first query has just refreshed that user's permissions for the action. This removes the permission cache's protection for negative authorization checks and can create substantial database load when many resources are checked or filtered.

findings.title: Denial cache blocks permissions granted after an initial denial
findings.body: Check returns immediately from permDenialCache before re-querying permissions, while line 154 populates that cache after any fresh denial for the shortCacheTTL period. If a dashboard or folder is created, a creator permission is added, or an administrator grants access after an initial denied check, subsequent identical checks continue to return false without consulting the database until the denial expires. An intervening check during creation can therefore poison access to the newly created resource and defeat the PR's intended fresh-permission re-query for up to the denial TTL.

findings.title: Denial cache key does not uniquely identify an authorization check
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, raw user UID, action, resource name, and parent with underscores, and its caller does not include the identity type. Anonymous and render subjects both use UID 0, so an anonymous denial can incorrectly deny the render service for the same action, resource, and folder even though the render service is granted read access. The ambiguous underscore encoding also makes distinct pairs such as name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' produce the same key. These collisions can incorrectly deny unrelated checks until the denial entry expires.

findings.title: Refreshed permission check still uses stale folder tree and then caches the denial
findings.body: After a cached check fails, Check re-runs checkPermission with refreshed permissions, but inherited-permission evaluation still uses buildFolderTree's cached folder tree and does not refresh or invalidate it. For a dashboard in a newly created folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor folder, the ancestor lookup can miss because the new folder is absent from the cached tree; the resulting false result is then stored in permDenialCache at line 154. This both prevents the permission re-query from fixing newly created nested resources in this case and can extend the incorrect denial beyond the folder cache's own expiry.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually prove the denial short-circuit
findings.body: The test comment says it allows access through permCache to prove that path is not checked, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. With that value, the cached-permission check would also deny, and the fallback fake store returns no permissions, so the test would still pass if the denial-cache early return were removed. The cached permission should be true and the test should preferably assert that the permission store is not consulted, so it genuinely verifies that a denial entry takes precedence.
